questions.q: What is the name of the fine, dust-like substance produced by the male part of a flower?
questions.a: It is called pollen. If a student answers "seed" or "nectar," they are confusing the reproductive materials with food rewards, suggesting they have not yet distinguished between the plant's reproductive organs and its attractants.

questions.q: Why do you think flowers have brightly coloured petals if their main job is to produce seeds?
questions.a: Bright petals attract pollinators like butterflies and bees, which help carry pollen between flowers. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks petals are just for decoration, failing to see the link between the plant's appearance and its survival strategy.

questions.q: If you carefully remove all the male parts (stamens) from a flower before it can produce its dust, what do you think will happen to the formation of seeds in that flower?
questions.a: The flower will likely fail to produce seeds because the male "dust" (pollen) is required for the female part to create a seed. A wrong answer indicates the student does not understand that both male and female components are necessary for the reproductive process.

questions.q: Compare the roles of the outer green parts of a flower and the central reproductive organs.
questions.a: The green parts protect the flower while it is a developing bud, while the central organs perform the actual work of reproduction. Confusing these two shows a lack of understanding of plant structure; the student likely sees the plant only as a static object rather than a growing, functioning system.

questions.q: Is a flower just a pretty decoration for a plant, or does it have a specific job to do? Justify your answer.
questions.a: It is a functional organ; it is the "nursery" where seeds are made. If a student says it is only for beauty, they ignore the biological necessity of reproduction for the plant's life cycle.

questions.q: If you were to design a flower that needs to attract a night-flying moth, what features would you give it, and why?
questions.a: The student should suggest features like white colour (visible at night) or a strong scent. A poor answer would suggest features useful for day-pollinators, showing they haven't grasped how plants adapt their reproductive structures to their environment.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Plant sexual ______ is the process in flowering plants where male and female parts of a flower interact to produce seeds, which then grow into new plants.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever wondered why a ______, colourful flower eventually disappears and a small fruit or seed pod appears in its place?
What is Plant sexual reproduction? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Plant sexual reproduction is the process in flowering plants where male and female parts of a flower interact to produce seeds, which then grow into new plants.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Plant sexual reproduction?
questions.a: Students often think that the "dust" (pollen) is "dirt" or "waste" that the plant wants to get rid of, rather than a vital component for reproduction.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify the male and female parts of a flower and explain the basic sequence that leads from pollination to seed formation.
